title: Tsukimi Japan's Moon-Viewing Tradition
paragraphs: Every autumn, people across Japan look up at the night sky to admire the full moon. This tradition, known as tsukimi or otsukimi, which means "moon viewing," has been celebrated for more than a thousand years.

The main night of tsukimi is called jugoya, which means "the fifteenth night." It takes place on the 15th day of the eighth month of the traditional lunar calendar. As a result, the date changes every year, usually falling in September or early October. In 2026, jugoya fell on September 25. A second, less well-known moon-viewing night, called jusanya, takes place about a month later. In 2026, it was held on October 23.

The custom is said to have begun during the Heian period, which lasted from the late eighth century to the late twelfth century. It was influenced by the Mid-Autumn Festival in China. During this period, members of the aristocracy gathered to write poetry under the moon, and some even held moon-viewing parties on boats so that they could see the moon's reflection on the water.

Today, the celebration is simpler. Many families decorate their homes with susuki, a type of pampas grass, and eat tsukimi dango, which are small, round rice dumplings that resemble the full moon. People also make offerings of seasonal foods, such as taro, edamame, chestnuts and sake. Because the festival is connected with the harvest, the full moon is sometimes called imomeigetsu, or "potato harvest moon." Interestingly, even when clouds or rain hide the moon, people still hold their parties.

The tradition has also influenced Japanese food. For example, tsukimi soba and tsukimi udon are noodle dishes topped with a raw egg, which looks like the moon. In autumn, some fast-food chains even sell "tsukimi burgers" that contain a fried egg.
Similar festivals are celebrated in other parts of Asia, including Chuseok in Korea and the Mid-Autumn Festival in China and Vietnam.
